newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Banks lead surge in Nigerian stock trade.
newsitem.headline: Banks lead surge in Nigerian stock trade.

text.p: Bank shares dominated the Nigerian stock market on Thursday after brewers set the pace the day before, dealers said.
The index closed at 8667.64 against Wednesday's 8632.42 on sustained demand for bank shares, they said.

"Government policy is creating a lot of interest in banks," said one trader, adding: "The sector will witness more activity both this year and in 1998 when a deadline on banks to raise their capital base by nine times will expire."
First Bank led the advance, closing 45 kobo up at 20.00 naira. Afribank was up 20 kobo at 9.75 naira and UBA rose 15 kobo to 14.30 naira.
Leading merchant bank NAL closed 15 kobo higher at 6.80 naira while FSB International Bank finished five kobo up at 3.25 naira.
Dealers said conglomerates surged on improving prospects. PZ Industries added 30 kobo to close at 27.40 naira while Lever Brothers rose 20 kobo to 27.30 naira.
UAC rose 20 kobo to 16.40 naira but Franco-Nigerian concern SCOA fell one kobo to 2.04 naira.
Continued dumping of National Salt Company of Nigeria was responsible for mixed trading in food/beverages sector, dealers said. The stock dropped 30 kobo to 5.80 naira.
Cadbury, after a lull on Wednesday, gained 30 kobo to 39.50 naira while Coca-Cola bottler the Nigerian Bottling Company ended 20 kobo higher at 52.50 naira.

Only Industrial Gases witnessed any movement in the industrial/domestic products sector, ending 15 kobo higher at 9.80 naira as investors, impressed with its recent performances, increased their holdings.
Weakening prices dominated the chemicals and paints sector where Berger Paints fell five kobo to 4.25 naira. Chemical and Allied Products slipped one kobo to 4.35 naira.
Buyers, however, raised the stake for International Paints of West Africa with a two kobo gain to 1.58 naira because they considered it a growth stock.
Oil marketing shares were unchanged because the fuel scarcity in some Nigerian cities which led stock traders to shun them persisted on Thursday.
